title: Roundup #90: In which Noah joins a Japanese VC firm
gist: Noah Smith's weekly roundup: he joins Japanese VC Coral Capital to push US capital into Japanese hard tech and defense; he challenges Paul Krugman's claim that data center spending is crowding out other investment; and he flags China's local-government debt crunch from collapsing land sales and China's loss of low-end manufacturing share to Bangladesh, Vietnam and Mexico. Smaller items cover AI as a vindication of financial capitalism, Japan's land readjustment, social media harms and rent control.

themes.theme: Japan hard-tech and defense investment thesis (Coral Capital)

insights.claim: Noah Smith is joining Japanese VC firm Coral Capital as a Venture Partner to encourage more American investment into Japan and help revitalize its economy.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Signals a prominent US commentator actively channeling US capital toward Japanese startups and defense tech.
insights.quote: I’ll be joining the Japanese VC firm Coral Capital as a Venture Partner!
insights.locator: I have a fun announcement today

insights.claim: Coral Capital argues the world's investment focus is shifting from bits back to atoms, with reindustrialization, defense, energy, robotics and physical AI as the defining investment themes of the next decade, all of which play to Japan's strengths.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: Frames Japanese hard tech as a decade-long secular theme for allocators rotating into physical-economy sectors.
insights.quote: The world’s focus is shifting from bits back to atoms.
insights.locator: Long before we started working together

insights.claim: Coral Capital argues that in hard-tech industries, language and culture barriers matter less than monozukuri, Japan's accumulated process power and manufacturing know-how.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: Suggests Japan's traditional handicaps for foreign investors are less relevant in manufacturing-heavy sectors.
insights.locator: Long before we started working together

insights.claim: As the world de-risks from Chinese supply chains, Coral Capital sees a once-in-a-generation opportunity for Japan to deepen US ties and fill manufacturing voids left behind.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: Supply-chain de-risking from China is a tailwind for Japanese manufacturers and US-Japan corridor investments.
insights.quote: Japan has a once-in-a-generation opportunity to deepen its ties with the United States
insights.locator: Long before we started working together

insights.claim: Japan is the largest foreign direct investor in the United States, Japanese companies support more American manufacturing jobs than any other foreign investor, and Japan hosts more US service members than any other country.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: Underlines the depth of US-Japan economic and security interdependence.
insights.quote: It is the largest foreign direct investor in the United States
insights.locator: Japan is America’s most important ally.

insights.claim: Anduril is building in Japan, not just selling there, with plans to invest billions in manufacturing capacity in the country.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: Major US defense-tech capex into Japan supports the thesis of Japan as an allied defense manufacturing base.
insights.quote: Anduril is not just selling to Japan but building in Japan
insights.locator: This is the thesis we laid out

insights.claim: Coral Capital portfolio companies such as Kyoto Fusioneering, TeraWatt Technology, Ookuma Diamond Device and GITAI are cited as examples of Japanese hard tech going global.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: Names specific Japanese fusion, battery, diamond semiconductor and space-robotics startups to watch.
insights.locator: This is the thesis we laid out

insights.claim: Smith has argued that Japan's manufacturing prowess is one of the most underpriced assets in the global economy and that Japan can be America's arsenal.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A long-Japan industrials and defense stance from a widely read economist.
insights.quote: Japan’s manufacturing prowess is one of the most underpriced assets in the global economy
insights.locator: Noah is one of Japan’s greatest champions

insights.claim: Coral Capital declares that Japan's lost decades are over.
insights.speaker: Coral Capital
insights.so_what: A bullish regime-change call on Japan's growth trajectory.
insights.quote: The lost decades are over.
insights.locator: The lost decades are over.

insights.claim: Paul Krugman argues that the AI data center boom is driving up interest rates and crowding out investment in housing, offices, factories and everything else not AI-related.
insights.speaker: Paul Krugman
insights.so_what: If correct, AI capex would be a headwind for rate-sensitive non-AI construction and real estate.
insights.quote: the surge in AI spending is driving up interest rates and crowding out all other investment
insights.locator: Krugman’s data center crowd-out story is fishy

insights.claim: Smith, citing Alex Tabarrok, notes that Steve Rattner's chart shows about $51 billion of data center spending set against a roughly $120 billion fall in other spending, which is too large to be explained by crowd-out since upward-sloping supply implies only partial crowd-out.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The non-AI construction slump likely has causes other than AI capex, so AI spending is not simply zero-sum for the rest of the economy.
insights.quote: how is $51 billion of data center spending supposed to crowd out $120 billion of other spending?
insights.locator: But as Alex Tabarrok notes

insights.claim: The timing undercuts the crowd-out story: real interest rates rose mainly in 2022-23, while non-data-center construction fell off a cliff only around mid-2025, a three-year lag.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Investors should be skeptical of attributing the 2025 construction slump to AI-driven rate pressure.
insights.quote: Why would it take three years for rising rates to start crowding out non-data-center construction?
insights.locator: But as Tabarrok also points out

insights.claim: Crowd-out via forward-looking expectations of future data center spending pushing up rates is possible in principle, but would require rates to have risen before GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 made AI's importance widely apparent.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Provides a test for whether AI expectations are actually moving long rates.
insights.locator: Of course it’s possible that non-data-center investment

insights.claim: Charts showing data center spending rising while other investment falls are not sufficient evidence of significant crowd-out.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Cautions against simple narrative attributions of macro weakness to the AI boom.
insights.locator: That could be true, I suppose

insights.claim: Although China has strong state capacity, it has always been a low-tax country, and its local governments funded public goods and industrial policy largely by selling land and real estate rather than collecting taxes.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Explains why China's property slump directly hits public spending and industrial policy.
insights.locator: Because of the history of how Europe developed

insights.claim: China's property sales are crashing, sharply cutting local governments' income and pushing them deeply into debt.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Property weakness feeds directly into local fiscal stress and weaker local investment.
insights.quote: The country’s property sales are crashing
insights.locator: That strategy is now hitting a wall.

insights.claim: Shih and Elkobi find that by the end of 2025, average monthly debt servicing exceeded 50% of monthly budgetary and extrabudgetary income for all but seven Chinese provincial units.
insights.speaker: Shih and Elkobi
insights.so_what: A concrete measure of how severe Chinese local-government debt stress has become.
insights.quote: by the end of 2025, average monthly debt servicing had surpassed 50 per cent of monthly budgetary and extrabudgetary income for all but seven Chinese provincial units
insights.locator: Shih and Elkobi have a new paper

insights.claim: China's central government will cover local governments' bills only reluctantly, since it is itself heavily indebted.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Limits the scale and speed of any fiscal bailout or stimulus via localities.
insights.locator: The central government will pick up the bill

insights.claim: China is likely to become increasingly centralized, ending the provincial autonomy that drove its dynamism in the 1990s, 2000s and early 2010s.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Less local experimentation could mean a structurally slower, more top-down Chinese growth model.
insights.locator: The upshot here is twofold.

insights.claim: China's local governments will be too debt-burdened to do much for a few years, ending their role as one of the strongest engines of China's growth.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Bearish for Chinese infrastructure-driven demand and commodities linked to local investment.
insights.quote: China’s local governments were one of its strongest engines of growth during the long boom, but that era looks like it’s over now.
insights.locator: The upshot here is twofold.

insights.claim: Despite Chinese leadership's goal of keeping labor-intensive industries at home (the 'China Squeeze'), China is losing market share in many labor-intensive manufacturing industries, per Kyle Chan's data.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: The China Squeeze is failing, so other developing economies still have an industrialization path.
insights.quote: Except the China Squeeze doesn’t seem to be succeeding.
insights.locator: A lot of people are saying that China

insights.claim: Bangladesh, Vietnam and Mexico, along with some European countries, are the main gainers of the labor-intensive manufacturing share China is losing.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports manufacturing-relocation plays in Vietnam, Mexico and Bangladesh.
insights.locator: And which countries are gaining

insights.claim: The outmigration of low-value labor-intensive manufacturing behaves like a law of nature that the CCP can slow but not halt, contrary to pundits who assume the Chinese state is industrially omnipotent.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Investors should not overestimate Beijing's ability to defy comparative-advantage shifts.
insights.quote: the outmigration of low-value labor-intensive manufacturing industries looks like a law of nature that even the mighty CCP can slow, but not halt
insights.locator: Modern pundits often just assume

themes.theme: AI and the vindication of financial capitalism

insights.claim: Epoch AI data shows the cost of each AI task falling dramatically every year.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rapid AI cost deflation expands addressable use cases.
insights.locator: The speed of AI progress has been truly dizzying.

insights.claim: Karthik Tadepalli estimates that measured relative to the amount spent on AI research, AI's cost declines are less exceptional, implying much of the progress comes from unprecedented spending.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: AI progress is capital-driven, so continued improvement depends on sustained capex.
insights.locator: But Karthik Tadepalli estimates

insights.claim: The AI boom is effectively spending the cash corporations accumulated over the previous decade and a half of hoarding.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Corporate cash piles are now being deployed into AI capex instead of sitting idle or going to buybacks.
insights.quote: we’ve been basically spending all the cash that we saved over the previous decade and a half of hoarding cash
insights.locator: In other words, a big reason AI

insights.claim: James Gilliland suggests that if AGI arrives, the resulting robotics-driven industrial boom will make the late 20th and early 21st centuries look like a capital-accumulation phase that vindicated neoliberalism, financialization and offshoring.
insights.speaker: James Gilliland
insights.so_what: A reframing of financialization as a precursor to AI-driven reindustrialization.
insights.quote: if we actually “get AGI,” the resulting boom in industrial capacity from robotics and massive society-wide wealth creation will look like a total vindication of neoliberalism
insights.locator: James Gilliland wonders if this was the plan

insights.claim: Smith suggests financial capitalism may have worked as textbook corporate finance predicts: firms like Google passed on poor pre-AI investment opportunities, then poured every dollar into AI once a good opportunity appeared.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Big Tech's shift from cash hoarding to massive AI capex is consistent with rational capital allocation, not a bubble by default.
insights.quote: Maybe companies like Google just looked at the available investment opportunities before AI and said “Nah”
insights.locator: Then AI came along

themes.theme: Housing policy: Japan land readjustment and rent control

insights.claim: Japanese cities build far more housing than US counterparts, and Japanese rents have not risen for a long time.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Shows supply-side housing policy can hold rents flat.
insights.locator: Going to Japan can be a radicalizing experience

insights.claim: Japan's 'land readjustment' redevelopment gives existing tenants a new home on the same spot at their previous rent, which, despite strong tenant protections, makes redevelopment easier than in the US.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A replicable model for unlocking dense redevelopment without displacing incumbents.
insights.quote: Japan actually has incredibly strong tenant protections.
insights.locator: One of his sources is this World Bank case study

insights.claim: Japan uses land readjustment instead of eminent domain for infrastructure, so no one is expropriated; landowners only compromise on plot size and proximity.
insights.speaker: Cremieux
insights.so_what: Lower-conflict land assembly could speed infrastructure delivery.
insights.quote: With land readjustment, no one is expropriated.
insights.locator: Cremieux then goes on to explain

insights.claim: Japan manages NIMBYs as stakeholders rather than steamrolling or kowtowing to them, which helps it build.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Political process design, not just zoning, drives housing supply.
insights.locator: How do they do it?

insights.claim: A synthesis of 112 studies by John Burn-Murdoch shows rent control helps existing covered tenants but reduces new construction, raises nearby rents, worsens homelessness and leads to property decay.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rent control regimes are negative for housing supply and landlord-maintained asset quality.
insights.locator: John Burn-Murdoch did the Lord’s work

insights.claim: Smith argues policymakers should drop rent control and instead build much more housing and hand out housing vouchers to the poor.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Supports pro-supply housing policy as the preferred affordability lever.
insights.quote: Just build a lot more housing and hand out housing vouchers to the poor.
insights.locator: I know lots of people love rent control

themes.theme: Society: humanities decline and social media

insights.claim: Ober et al.'s 'The Humanities in Crisis' shows US humanities dissertations declining for over a decade, while the social sciences decline began only post-pandemic.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Reduces risk of the 'elite overproduction' dynamic Smith blamed for 2010s unrest.
insights.locator: From a new study called

insights.claim: Smith suspects poor job prospects for humanities PhDs, more than wokeness, drive the decline, since fewer undergrads major in the humanities, reducing demand for professors and grad students.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Labor-market signals are reshaping higher-education demand.
insights.locator: Why this is happening is not clear yet.

insights.claim: Smith argues that overproduction of humanities scholars will no longer be a significant source of elite overproduction and social unrest going forward.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Removes one structural driver of political instability Smith previously identified.
insights.locator: But whether or not that argument was right

insights.claim: Pew data shows growing shares of people, especially in developed countries, view social media as bad for democracy.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Rising public hostility raises regulatory risk for social media platforms.
insights.locator: As someone who has been shouting

insights.claim: Greece's legislature passed a ban on social media for children under 15, an example of age-based restrictions Smith favors.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Child social-media bans are spreading, a regulatory headwind for platforms' youth engagement.
insights.quote: Greece is leading the charge
insights.locator: What can we do about the problem?
